# Tidal Locking and the Shaping of Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among planets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in perpetual starlight, can reach temperatures hot enough to vaporize rock on close-orbiting worlds, while the nightside plunges to hundreds of degrees below zero. Without atmospheric redistribution, this divide would render most of the planet uninhabitable.

However, atmospheres and oceans act as planetary climate equalizers. Winds transport heat from the dayside toward the nightside, while ocean currents—particularly on water worlds—can moderate temperatures even more effectively. Climate models suggest that planets with thick atmospheres or substantial oceans may maintain habitable conditions across much of their surface, with the terminator zone, the twilight band between day and night, offering especially temperate conditions.

Tidal locking also drives unique weather patterns. The constant heating of the dayside creates persistent updrafts and a permanent low-pressure system, while the nightside develops high pressure. This can generate supersonic winds on some worlds and stable, permanent cloud formations that may even reflect enough starlight to cool the dayside significantly.
